items.t: Crop model 11.63m bales vs USDA 13.44m (-14%), driven by Texas abandonment of 52% vs USDA's 34% on drought and poor ratings. A cut that size after the October report has happened once since 2010/11 (2020/21, -14%), so the model sits near the edge of history.

Watch: West Texas-Kansas-Oklahoma (production estimates falling, fiber quality concerns, regrowth, insurance adjusters in fields, some gins not opening); Desert Southwest (DSW) (storm damage being assessed); American Pima (AP) (storm damage being assessed). Harvest (NASS, as quoted): Alabama 38%, Georgia 26%, Virginia 27%, Carolinas 16%, Arkansas 63%, Missouri 42%, Tennessee 46%, Louisiana 72%, Mississippi 70%.

Demand: export slow to moderate; finished-product (yarn/fabric) demand slow; export inquiries from Thailand, Vietnam, Mexico, Peru, Korea, Pakistan. Domestic mill buyers inquired for a moderate volume of color 41 and better, leaf 4 and better, and staple 36 and longer for December 2026 through December 2027 delivery.
25% of US acres contracted as of 2026-09-30 vs 17% a year ago and a 16% five-season average; Texas 36%. More of the crop is priced early, leaving less grower selling for later.
Export sales (week 12) project 12.61 m bales vs USDA 12.30 (+3%); commitments +17% vs a year ago. Outlook above USDA's 12.30 m bales.

India's crop looks like 21.0 m bales on the desk model (USDA 24.0) after the driest June–September in its main cotton districts since at least 1991. With the import duty waived to 2026-12-31 India imports about 4.5 m bales (5.3 m if the waiver runs all season) vs USDA's 3.3 m. US cotton to India: 0.9–1.5 m bales against 0.28 m committed, so 0.7–1.2 m of new US sales are still to come. Counting the Brazilian, African and Australian cotton India takes from other buyers, US exports gain about 0.4 m bales in the desk base and 1.0 m in the bearish (big-crop, lower-price) case; in the desk's simulated balance sheet (crop and exports drawn together, India's duty path included) base exports are 12.9 m vs USDA 12.3, ending stocks 2.3 m (bullish 1.5, bearish 3.9; USDA 3.80), and 89% of runs end below USDA. At today's prices more of this demand gets booked, so the tightness should show in flat price first; in past seasons tight US stocks alone did not invert Mar/May (-1.64) or May/Jul (-0.47) — that took a world shortage (2010/11, 2021/22) — and Jul/Dec (+6.64) already prices the tight case.
Desk base case 2026/27 ending stocks 2.32 vs USDA 3.80 (stocks/use 16.1% vs 27.5%); bearish 3.86, bullish 1.50.

On the desk base case history points May (now 83.89) to about 91 by expiry; the simulation gives 77–103 (10th–90th percentile), a 77% chance May trades 90 or higher and 38% that it trades 78 or lower along the way. Merchants' shorts are 54% of world exports, the most at this time of year since 2010/11; in heavily hedged seasons May rose 19% on average. Spreads: Mar/May -1.64 should stay a carry (median -2.2 near expiry), May/Jul -0.47 has a 22% chance of inverting, and Jul/Dec +6.64 is already above what US stocks alone justify (median +2.5 by June) unless world supply turns short.
